The commentators explain that the one who will truly burn in the blazing fire is the most wretched, namely the one who denied the truth and turned away from obedience. Their wording differs on the two terms. Qatada and others take the denial to be of the Book of God and the turning away to be from His obedience, while others read it as denial of the Messenger and refusal to follow him. Al-Farra' holds that this denial is not an open rejection but a failure to obey, called denial by figure of speech. Ibn Kathir adds that it is denial in the heart and turning away in deeds. Ibn 'Abbas restricts the verse to Umayya ibn Khalaf and those like him who denied the prophets, whereas Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi generally apply it to the unbeliever.

The question of major sins drew much attention. Al-Zajjaj, al-Farra' and al-Razi report the argument of the Murji'a that only the unbeliever enters the Fire, and answer that this is a specific fire, and that the people of the Fire have different levels, as the verse on the hypocrites in the lowest level shows. Al-Razi explains that the meaning is not being durably scorched, so that the sinner either does not enter or leaves it. Al-Zamakhshari sees the verse as a contrast between two extremes.

The scholars agree that the most pious person who is kept far from the Fire is first of all Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and that the verse extends to anyone who gives his wealth to purify himself seeking the face of his Lord. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur hold a general application. Some report accounts of the occasion of revelation linked to the freeing of Bilal, and al-Qurtubi notes the variant readings of the verse.

This verse says that only the most wretched, the disbeliever who denied the truth and turned away from it, will burn in the blazing fire, while the most God-fearing will be kept far from it. The verse describes the latter as one who gives his wealth to purify himself, seeking the face of his Lord and not repaying any favour. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi, identify the most God-fearing as Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, citing Ibn Abbas and others, who freed Bilal and other slaves tortured for their faith; the Meccans claimed he did so out of gratitude for a favour, which the verse denies. Al-Zamakhshari reads the verse as a contrast between a great sinner among the polytheists and a great believer, while Ibn Kathir and al-Qasimi say it applies to anyone with these qualities, Abu Bakr being the foremost. Al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi note that some scholars read the two superlatives as simply meaning the wretched and the pious. The preceding verse, about wealth not helping one when he perishes, is explained by Qatada and Abu Salih as falling into hell, and by Mujahid as dying; al-Tabari prefers the first reading. Al-Baghawi and al-Farra' explain that 'guidance belongs to Us' means God makes clear the path of right and wrong. Some commentators, including Ibn Ashur, observe that the verse's apparent restriction of the blazing fire to unbelievers raised questions, which later scholars addressed in differing ways.

This verse states that God guides people by sending messengers and scriptures, and that the Hereafter and this world belong to Him. It then warns of a blazing Fire that only the most wretched will enter, the one who denied and turned away, while the most righteous will be kept far from it. Commentators differ on the meaning of "al-ashqa" and "al-atqa". Al-Zamakhshari and others take them as the absolute extremes of wretchedness and piety, while al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir understand them as the disbeliever set against the most God-fearing. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain "taraddaa" as falling into hellfire, whereas Mujahid takes it to mean dying.

Most exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Razi, report that these verses were revealed about Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who freed Bilal and other persecuted slaves. The polytheists claimed he did so out of a debt of gratitude, and the verse denies this, since he gave seeking only the face of his Lord. Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi explain that "yatazakka" means purifying oneself or growing in God's sight, free of showing off. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that spending should be moderate, neither wasteful nor stingy, and that borrowing money to give charity is not permitted.

Other points are also noted, such as the variant reading "tatalazzaa" and the grammatical role of the verb as an adverbial clause or a substitute. Al-Mawardi lists several meanings of "guidance" and "taraddaa", while Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qasimi stress God's responsibility to make the right path clear.

This passage of Surat al-Layl says that God takes charge of guiding people to the right path, and warns of a blazing Fire that only the most wretched will enter, namely the disbeliever who denies and turns away. The most God-fearing will be kept far from it, the one who gives of his wealth to purify himself. The commentators agree that the first person meant by the most God-fearing is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the verse was revealed about his freeing of Bilal; the Quraysh claimed he did it out of a past favour owed to him, and the verse denies that anyone is owed a favour by him. According to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, the giving is spontaneous, sought for the face of God alone. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take the word "except" as a disconnected exception, while al-Farra and al-Nahhas treat the phrase as an object of purpose. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari also hold that the most God-fearing is rewarded with being pleased. Ibn Kathir holds that the verse is general, with Abu Bakr its foremost example. Al-Zamakhshari sees the two extremes as a deliberate contrast. Ibn Kathir and al-Zajjaj note that the Fire is not reserved for the disbeliever alone, since the damned have different ranks.

This verse describes the God-fearing person who spends his wealth without seeking to repay any favour he received. He gives only to seek the countenance of his Lord, the Most High, meaning His pleasure and reward. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy, read the particle 'illa' as 'but rather', making the phrase an exceptive clause of disconnection. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud note that it can also be read as an object of purpose, and Ibn Juzayy observes that the nominative reading attributed to Yahya ibn Wathhab follows a known Arabic usage. Nearly all the commentators report that the surah was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who freed Bilal and other persecuted slaves, and that the Quraysh claimed he did so only out of gratitude for a past favour, which the verse denies. Ibn Kathir sees in these verses the qualities that make Abu Bakr the foremost of this community, while al-Razi argues that his station is higher because he gave without hope of reward or fear of punishment. Al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di extend the meaning to every believer, Ibn Sa'di adding that no one can repay the Prophet's own favour of guidance. Other reports cited by al-Qurtubi and al-Tha'alibi link the revelation to Abu al-Dahdah, but the account about Abu Bakr remains the most widely accepted among the commentators.

This verse says that the one who gives purely, seeking nothing in return from anyone and desiring only the face of his Lord, the Most High, will be promised a reward in the hereafter that will fully satisfy him. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, report that it was revealed about Abu Bakr when he freed Bilal, in answer to those who claimed his act repaid an earlier favour from Bilal. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi also cite another report that links the verse to Abu al-Dahdah and his date palm. On the grammar of the exception "except seeking the face of his Lord", al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari present several readings: most take it as a detached exception meaning "but", al-Farra' and those who follow him take it as an object of purpose, and Yahya ibn Wathhab reads it in the nominative as the Tamim dialect allows. As for who is satisfied, most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di, understand the giver to be satisfied with his reward, while al-Razi holds that God is pleased with him, which he regards as the higher meaning. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the verse covers anyone who acts in the same way, with Abu Bakr as the foremost of them.
